p: Most trimming on a tree crew is light work: tidying edges after a removal, knocking down weeds around a stump before grinding, clearing a path to a backyard tree so the crew can haul brush. You do not need premium line for that. A good general-purpose Husqvarna trimmer line cuts cleanly, feeds without jamming and costs less per foot.
Save heavier reinforced line for fence lines, rocky ground and woody brush where standard line snaps too often.
For a crew, the cost of line adds up quickly over a season. A reliable everyday line that does not jam or weld on the spool saves more time than a premium line used where it is not needed.

Line diameter is the first thing to get right. Use the size your head is designed for. Too heavy and the engine labors, the clutch heats up and the head wears early. Too light and the line breaks constantly and cuts poorly in thick grass.

Most bump heads list a maximum size on the head or in the manual. Fixed-line heads may need pre-cut lengths. If you run several trimmers, standardize on one size where you can so one spool covers the fleet.
Gas trimmers on a tree crew often double as brushcutters for clearing access. When that is the job, switch to a blade or a heavier line rated for the head, and always use the matching guard.
Wind line tight and even in the direction marked on the spool and leave a little room at the top. Overfilled spools jam. Trim the tip at an angle to make threading easier.

Line dries out and gets brittle in sun and heat. Keep it in its packaging or a sealed bag, out of the cab dash, and rotate stock so old line gets used first. A brief soak in water before loading can help stiff line feed better.
If the head keeps jamming even with good line, check the spool and eyelets for wear. Grooved eyelets cut line and worn bump knobs stop feeding properly; both are cheap parts to replace.

If you find yourself stopping every few minutes to bump out new line, it is worth stepping up to Husqvarna Titanium X-Pro trimmer line, which is built to last longer on hard surfaces. Whatever line you run, wear eye and hearing protection, use the trimmer guard and keep people well clear of the thrown debris. More cleanup gear is in our landscaper tools section.
Keeping one everyday line and one heavy-duty line on the truck lets the crew match the line to the job without overpaying on routine trimming.

faq.q: What is the difference between TrimForce and Titanium line?
faq.a: TrimForce is an everyday line for grass and weeds. Titanium line is reinforced for longer wear on fences, rock and heavy growth.

faq.q: Does Husqvarna trimmer line fit other brands?
faq.a: Yes. Trimmer line is not brand-specific; just match the diameter to your head.

faq.q: Why does my line keep welding together on the spool?
faq.a: Usually heat and a loose wind. Wind it tighter, avoid overfilling and let the head cool between heavy cuts.

name: Notch Fusion Rope Wrench Tether
title: Notch Fusion Rope Wrench Tether: Replacement Tether
h1: Notch Fusion Rope Wrench Tether
meta: The Notch Fusion rope wrench tether is a replacement tether for your Rope Wrench SRS setup. Swap a worn tether and keep your stationary rope system dialed.
tagline: Replacement tether that links a Rope Wrench to your friction hitch on SRS.
summary: The Notch Fusion rope wrench tether is the short connecting link between a Rope Wrench and your hitch on a stationary rope system. Tethers wear and fatigue with use, and swapping in a fresh one is cheap insurance.
highlights: Replacement tether for Rope Wrench SRS setups
Stiff, consistent length for smooth tending
Sewn terminations
Easy swap during routine gear inspection
Keep a spare in the gear bag

p: On a Rope Wrench system the tether holds the wrench a set distance above your friction hitch. The wrench adds friction and keeps the hitch from grabbing in descent, and the tether is what lets the wrench follow you up and down the rope. A tired, bent or worn tether changes how the system feels, and a damaged one can stop it working properly.
The Fusion tether is a straightforward replacement. Match it to your device and setup, and check that the length works with your hitch.
Many climbers carry a spare tether in the gear bag. If you find damage during the morning inspection, a quick swap keeps you climbing instead of sending you back to the shop.

Inspect the tether each day with the rest of your life-support gear. Retire it if the cover is cut, glazed or worn through, stitching is damaged, or it has taken a shock load. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the wrench and tether, and have your system set up and checked by someone qualified.
SRS is life-support climbing. Be trained on it before you use it, and test every setup close to the ground. See other devices for SRS if you are building a new system.

faq.q: How often should I replace my rope wrench tether?
faq.a: Whenever inspection shows wear, cuts, glazing or stitching damage, or after a shock load. Heavy users often replace it regularly.

faq.q: Is the tether part of life-support gear?
faq.a: Yes. Treat it like the rest of your climbing system and inspect it before every climb.

name: Polymer Tool Hook with Standard End
title: Polymer Saddle Hook for Pruning Hooks, Saws and Tools
h1: Polymer Tool Hook for Pruning Hooks and Saws
meta: A light polymer saddle hook for carrying pruning hooks, pole saws and hand saws aloft. Keeps tools within reach on the saddle and off your life-support gear.
tagline: A simple polymer hook for hanging pruning tools on your saddle.
summary: This polymer hook clips to your saddle so pruning hooks, pole saw heads and hand saw scabbards have a home that is not your life-support hardware. It is light, quiet against the rope and cheap enough to run a few.
highlights: Lightweight polymer, quiet and kind to ropes
Standard end attaches to saddle tool loops
Holds pole pruners, pruning hooks and saws
Keeps tools off your climbing carabiners
Not rated for life support

body.h: Why carry tools on a hook
p: Pruning work means switching between hand saw, pole saw and pruning hooks all day. Each tool needs a place on the saddle where you can grab it one-handed and put it back without looking. Hanging them off a life-support carabiner or a D-ring is a bad habit; a dedicated tool hook keeps the gear organized and keeps your climbing hardware clear.
A polymer hook is light and does not clank or scratch other hardware. It also will not damage your rope if it bumps against it while you move through the canopy.

Pruning hooks, pole saw heads and long-handled loppers are the hardest tools to carry well. They are too long for a scabbard and too awkward to hold while you move. A dedicated hook gives them a resting spot between cuts, so both hands are free for climbing and positioning.

Think about where each tool needs to be. Most climbers carry the hand saw on the hip of their non-dominant side, with a hook further back for a pole pruner or pruning hook head when it is not in hand. Long tools ride better hanging vertically from a hook at the rear of the saddle so they do not catch on limbs.
Run a short lanyard or tool leash for pole saws and pruning hooks so a slip does not send them to the ground. Anything that falls lands in the drop zone, so keep the ground crew clear while you work.

Spread the load. Putting every tool on one side pulls the saddle off center and makes it harder to sit level in the bridge. Balance the weight left and right, and keep the heaviest items close to your hips.

Pole pruners and pruning hooks are sharp, long and awkward. Carry them with the blade pointed down and away from your rope and lanyard, and never let a blade rest against any part of your climbing system. When you hand-line a tool up, send it on a separate line and clip it to the hook only after you have control of it.
If your work is near power lines, use only insulated tools and qualified line-clearance methods. Metal hooks and poles conduct.

This is a storage hook, not climbing hardware. Never use it to connect yourself, your lanyard or your rope, or to hold rigging loads. Replace it if it cracks, bends or loses its shape. For rated connectors and more storage options, browse our saddle storage section.
Check the attachment point on the saddle as well. Tool loops wear and can tear from constant weight, so inspect them along with the hook and move the hook if the loop shows damage.

faq.q: Can this hook hold a pole saw?
faq.a: Yes, it is meant to carry tools such as pole saws and pruning hooks on your saddle. Keep the blade pointed away from your climbing system.

faq.q: Is a polymer hook rated for climbing?
faq.a: No. It is for tool storage only and must never be used as part of your life-support system.

faq.q: How many tool hooks should I run?
faq.a: Most climbers use two or three, placed so each tool has its own spot and can be reached one-handed.

name: Stars and Stripes Adjustable Friction Saver
title: Stars and Stripes Adjustable Friction Saver
h1: Stars and Stripes Adjustable Friction Saver
meta: An adjustable friction saver in a stars and stripes rope pattern. Sizes to the limb, protects bark and your climbing line, and retrieves from the ground.
tagline: An adjustable rope friction saver that fits small leaders and big unions alike.
summary: An adjustable friction saver lets you size the sling to the limb you are tying in on instead of carrying several fixed lengths. This Stars and Stripes version uses a patriotic rope pattern that is easy to spot in the canopy.
highlights: Adjustable length to suit small and large tie-in points
Rope construction with rings for low friction
Protects bark and reduces wear on your climbing line
Retrievable from the ground when set up properly
Easy-to-spot stars and stripes pattern
specs: Length adjusts to the tie-in point

p: When a climbing line runs directly over a limb, the rope and the bark both pay for it. Every ascent and descent saws the rope across the wood, cambium gets burned and the line heats up and wears. A friction saver puts rings at the tie-in point so the rope runs through metal instead of over bark. Your ascent gets smoother, your rope lasts longer, and the tree is not scarred.

Fixed friction savers come in set lengths, so one might be too short for a big union and too long for a small leader. An adjustable friction saver solves that by letting you shorten or lengthen the body to fit the limb.

This style uses a rope body with a large ring and a small ring. One end of the body is adjustable, typically using a hitch or sliding eye arrangement, so you can take up slack around a tight crotch or let out length for a wide limb. Set it so the rings sit level on top of the limb and close together, not hanging down the sides.

Many climbers install it from the ground with a throw line and retrieve it the same way. Practice the install and retrieve low to the ground before you rely on it, because a badly rigged retrieve can leave it stuck in the tree.

Watch the ring sizes when you set it. The large ring must be able to pass through the small ring for a ground retrieval to work, and your climbing hitch or knot must not jam in the rings. Check that the rings are not cross-loaded against bark or the stem.

A friction saver does not make a weak limb strong. Pick a sound, live union of adequate diameter, high and central enough to give a good working angle. Look for decay, cracks and included bark, and test the anchor with body weight before committing. A Zing-It throw line makes setting the saver at height much easier.
On SRS, consider the load on the anchor and the redirect forces, and follow your system's instructions for using rings or an anchor sling.
Remember that the friction saver is part of the anchor. If you set it on a limb that later fails, the friction saver goes with it. Take time to assess the tree before every climb.

Inspect the rope body, stitching or splices and rings before every climb. Retire it if the cover is cut, glazed or fuzzed through, if rings are grooved or cracked, or after any shock load. Friction savers are life-support gear: check that yours meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and get trained on its use. See more options in our friction savers section.

faq.q: What is an adjustable friction saver used for?
faq.a: It protects the tree and your climbing line at the tie-in point, and it can be lengthened or shortened to fit different limb sizes.

faq.q: Can I install it from the ground?
faq.a: Yes, with a throw line, as long as it is rigged correctly so it can be retrieved. Practice low first.

faq.q: Can I use it for SRS?
faq.a: Many climbers do, but check the manufacturer's instructions and make sure the anchor and configuration suit the loads of your system.

name: Samson Zing-It Throw Line, 180 ft.
title: Samson Zing-It Throw Line, 180 ft.: Setting Lines High
h1: Samson Zing-It Throw Line, 180 ft.
meta: Samson Zing-It throw line in a 180 ft. length: slick, strong Dyneema line that slides over limbs and through crotches for setting climbing lines high.
tagline: Slick, low-friction throw line for setting climbing and rigging lines high.
summary: Samson Zing-It throw line is the slick, thin line many climbers reach for when they need to set a climbing line through a high crotch. The 180 ft. length covers most residential and many large shade trees with line to spare.
highlights: Dyneema (HMPE) construction with a slick coating
Slides easily over bark and through tight unions
Low stretch for control when isolating limbs
180 ft. length suits most climbing trees
Bright colors for spotting in the canopy

p: Setting a good line is the first job of every climb, and the throw line is the tool that does it. Zing-It is made from a coated Dyneema fiber that is slick and thin, so it slides over bark and through narrow crotches with very little friction. That makes it easier to isolate the union you want and to pull the climbing line through without the throw line hanging up.
It is also low stretch. When you are working a throw weight across a limb to isolate a tie-in point, the line responds to small inputs instead of bouncing.

Because it is so slick, Zing-It also comes down out of the tree cleanly when you pull a line back, with fewer snags on bark and small branches. That saves time on big jobs where you set several lines in the same tree.

Pair Zing-It with a throw weight sized to the job, often 8 to 14 oz depending on height and the density of the canopy. Lighter weights travel further for a given throw and come down through small branches; heavier weights pull line down more reliably through foliage. Many climbers carry two of each.

Store the line in a throw cube or bag so it pays out cleanly. Flake it in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep sticks and sawdust out. Use a big-shot or slingshot launcher for very tall trees, following its safety instructions.
Mark the end of the line that ties to the weight and the end that stays in the bag, and tie a stopper knot at the bag end so the whole line does not follow a long throw into the crown.

Once you are over the right union, tie the climbing line on with a secure hitch and pull it up and over smoothly. Pull steadily; jerking the line is how you snap a branch or get a hang-up. If you set a friction saver from the ground, the throw line carries it up into position and later helps retrieve it.
Keep the throw zone clear. Weights coming down are hard and fast, and everyone on the ground needs to know when you are throwing. Wear a helmet and eye protection while throwing.

Zing-It is a throw line, never a climbing or rigging line, and never life support. Check it for fuzzing, glazed sections and cuts, and cut out damaged sections. Heat from fast pulls over rough bark can glaze the coating, so pull steadily. A 180 ft. hank lets you cut out bad sections and still have plenty to work with.
Wash muddy line in a bucket of cool water and let it dry fully before packing it away. Grit trapped in the fibers wears the coating and makes it grab.

faq.q: What throw weight should I use with Zing-It?
faq.a: Most climbers use weights from about 8 to 14 oz, lighter for height and open canopies, heavier for pulling line down through dense foliage.

faq.q: Can I use throw line for rigging?
faq.a: No. Throw line is only for setting other lines. It is not rated for rigging or life support.

faq.q: Is 180 ft. enough throw line?
faq.a: For most trees, yes. Very tall trees and launcher work may need more.

name: Clogger Zero Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger Zero Chainsaw Pants: Light Saw Pants for Climbing
h1: Clogger Zero Chainsaw Pants
meta: Clogger Zero chainsaw pants pair leg protection with a light, cool, stretch build that moves with a saddle. Fit, care and who they suit, from tree crews.
tagline: Light, breathable chainsaw pants built so climbers actually keep them on.
summary: Clogger Zero chainsaw pants put leg protection inside a light, breathable pant that moves with a climbing saddle. They are aimed at climbers and sawyers in warm weather who have given up on heavy saw pants.
highlights: Lightweight, breathable build for hot-weather climbing
Stretch panels for high steps and saddle work
Cut protection across the front of the legs
Fits under a saddle without bunching
Made by Clogger, known for comfort-first saw protection

p: Chaps work on the ground, but in a saddle they bunch, twist and catch on stubs. That is why most climbers who protect their legs in the tree wear chainsaw pants. The protective layers sit inside the pant, so nothing flaps around while you move through the crown.

The problem has always been heat. Traditional saw pants are heavy and hot, and on a July removal plenty of climbers skip them. Clogger built the Zero line to be light and breathable enough that you will wear it on those days, which is when protection matters most.

Ground crews benefit too. Bucking and limbing on a hot day in heavy chaps wears you down, and comfortable saw pants that move with you help you stay focused and keep your footing while you work through a pile.

Try the pants with your saddle and spurs on. Leg loops and bridges sit over the pant, so you want enough room in the seat and thigh to step high and sit back without the fabric pulling tight. Stretch panels help, and suspender buttons keep the waist where it should be when you hang in the saddle all day.
Length matters on spurs. Too long and the hem catches on the gaff straps, too short and your boot top is exposed. Check the length with the boots you climb in.
Pick a size based on the waist and inseam you actually wear with layers underneath. Many climbers size so they can wear thin base layers in winter without the pants getting tight.

Like other saw pants, the Zero uses layers of long fibers behind the outer shell. When a running chain cuts through the shell, the fibers pull out and jam the sprocket to slow or stop the chain. That only works if the pants are in good condition, and only on the protected area, which is mainly the front of the legs.

Saw pants reduce injury; they do not make a saw safe. Good technique, sharp chains, a working chain brake and training are still the main protection. Keep using a top-handle saw only as the manufacturer and your training allow.

Wash per the label to clear out oil and sawdust, which can reduce how well the protective fibers pull out. Replace the pants after any cut through the outer layer into the protective layer, even a small one. For ground-only work, compare Clogger Zero apron chaps, and see the premium Clogger Zero Ultra for more features.
Clogger pants can be worn in cool weather too. Add a thin base layer underneath rather than wearing a bulky pair of insulated pants, which can affect fit and freedom of movement.

faq.q: Are Clogger Zero chainsaw pants good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. They are designed to be light and flexible enough to wear in a saddle all day.

faq.q: Do saw pants protect the back of the legs?
faq.a: Most protection is on the front of the legs. Check the label for the exact coverage of your pair.

faq.q: Can I repair cut saw pants?
faq.a: No. A cut into the protective layer means the pants should be retired.

name: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks
title: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks for Lanyards and Slings
h1: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks
meta: Edelrid static rope shorty hanks are short pre-cut lengths of low-stretch rope, ideal for building flip lines, adjustable slings and short lowering lines.
tagline: Short lengths of Edelrid static rope for lanyards, slings and rigging bits.
summary: Edelrid static rope shorty hanks are short lengths of low-stretch kernmantle rope cut from full spools. They are the cheap, practical way to get quality rope for a flip line, a sling or a short lowering line without buying a 150 ft. hank.
highlights: Short pre-cut lengths of Edelrid static rope
Low-stretch kernmantle construction
Good stock for lanyards, slings and lowering lines
Cheaper than cutting from a full spool
Ends sealed for handling

p: Every gear room ends up needing short pieces of good rope. A new flip line, a sling to choke a limb, a short lowering line for the bucket truck, a tag line on a small rigging job. Buying a full spool for those jobs is wasteful, and cutting up a retired climbing line gives you worn rope. Shorty hanks fill the gap.

These are short lengths of Edelrid static rope. Static kernmantle rope has low stretch, a firm hand and a cover that holds up well against bark and hardware, which makes it a good base for positioning and light rigging uses.

Shorty hanks are a smart way to try a rope before you commit to a full climbing line or rigging spool. Build a lanyard from a hank and you will learn how the rope handles, how it takes a hitch and how the cover wears.

If you are making a positioning lanyard, you need a termination your system is designed for, such as a sewn eye, a properly tied and dressed knot or a splice made by a trained splicer. Pair the rope with an adjuster or hitch cord that is rated for its diameter. Never mix gear outside the manufacturers' compatibility lists.
For rigging, a short hank works well as a choker sling with a tied or spliced eye, or as a light lowering line on small pieces. Know the rope's strength and keep loads well within working limits.

Size the hank to the job. A flip line needs enough length to go around the largest stems you climb plus the tails for the adjuster and termination. A choker only needs enough to wrap the limb and leave a tail to tie off.

Rope you make into life-support gear must meet the applicable standard for that use, and the finished item, including terminations, has to be suitable. If you are not trained to build and inspect lanyards, buy a finished one. ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions apply. Inspect every homemade piece before each use and retire it at the first sign of damage.
Mark shorty hanks with their length and date when you cut them up, so you know how old each piece is and what it came from.

Keep rope out of sun, heat and chemicals, especially bar oil and fuel. Store hanks coiled in a bag, not loose in the truck bed with saws and wedges. Wash in cool water with a rope cleaner if they get heavily soiled. Compare with the other Edelrid shorty hank listing for different lengths or colors.
If you are not sure what to build from a hank, start with a tag line or a choker. These are simple, useful uses that build familiarity with the rope.

faq.q: What can I make from a shorty hank?
faq.a: Common uses are flip lines, chokers and slings, tag lines and short lowering lines. Life-support items need proper terminations and training.

faq.q: Is static rope good for a flip line?
faq.a: Yes, low-stretch rope is a common choice for positioning lanyards when paired with a compatible adjuster and termination.

faq.q: Are shorty hanks cut from new rope?
faq.a: Shorty hanks are short lengths cut from spools. Check the listing for the exact length and color of each hank.

name: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks, Short Lengths
title: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks: Short Rope Lengths
h1: Edelrid Static Rope Shorty Hanks, Short Lengths
meta: Short lengths of Edelrid static rope in shorty hanks. Good value rope for tag lines, chokers, lowering lines and practice, without buying a full spool.
tagline: Short lengths of Edelrid static rope for lanyards, slings and rigging bits.
summary: Edelrid static rope in shorty hanks gives you real climbing-grade kernmantle rope in short lengths at a lower price. Crews use them as tag lines, chokers, short lowering lines and practice rope for knots and hitches.
highlights: Short pre-cut lengths of Edelrid static rope
Low-stretch kernmantle construction
Good stock for lanyards, slings and lowering lines
Cheaper than cutting from a full spool
Ends sealed for handling

p: Not every rope job needs a 150 ft. hank. Shorty hanks are short lengths of Edelrid static rope, the leftover footage from full spools. You get the same low-stretch construction and durable cover at a price that makes sense for the many small jobs a crew does every week.

Think of them as the utility drawer of the rope bag. A tag line to steer a piece clear of a roof, a quick choker to snatch a small limb, a pull line for a small felling cut, or a hank kept in the bucket truck for lowering small wood.
Because they come from good rope, shorty hanks hold up much better than hardware-store rope. The cover resists bark, the core stays round and knots untie after a load.

Shorty hanks are also good training rope. New climbers can practice knots, hitches and terminations at the shop or on the ground without tying up a working climbing line. Tie a running bowline, a clove hitch, a timber hitch and a figure eight on a bight until you can do them with gloves on and eyes closed.
Keep practice rope separate from working rope and mark it clearly, so it never ends up in the climb kit by accident.

Practice rope also helps when teaching the ground crew. Rigging knots, a proper bowline for a tag line and the hitches used on a lowering device are all worth learning, even for people who never climb.

Know the diameter and strength of the hank you have, and keep rigging loads well inside the rope's working limits. Short static rope does not absorb shock, so avoid letting pieces free-fall onto it. For anything bigger than small pieces, use a proper rigging line and lowering device.
If you plan to turn a hank into life-support gear, such as a lanyard, it must be suitable for that use, terminated correctly and built by someone trained to do it. When in doubt, buy finished gear.
Write the intended use on a tag at each end. A tag line and a practice rope can look identical in the bag, and labeling keeps the right rope on the right job.

Check the cover for cuts, glazing and core shots, and feel along the length for soft or stiff spots. Keep rope away from bar oil, fuel and battery acid. Store hanks dry and out of sun. For a hank sized for lanyards and slings, see our other Edelrid shorty hanks, and pull them up into the tree with a Zing-It throw line.
Coil each hank the same way every time so it pays out without tangles when you need it in a hurry.

faq.q: Why buy shorty hanks instead of a full spool?
faq.a: For tag lines, chokers and practice rope, short lengths cost less and you avoid cutting up a long working line.

faq.q: Can I use a shorty hank as a climbing line?
faq.a: Shorty hanks are generally too short to climb on. Use a full-length climbing line rated for life support.

faq.q: How do I seal a cut end?
faq.a: Use a hot knife or tape and heat-shrink the end so the cover and core do not unravel.

name: Masdaam Continuous Rope Puller Kit
title: Masdaam Rope Puller: Continuous Rope Puller Kit
h1: Masdaam Rope Puller Kit, Continuous Pull
meta: The Masdaam rope puller kit is a hand-operated continuous rope winch for directional felling, pulling over leaners and moving loads where a truck can't go.
tagline: A portable hand-operated rope winch for felling, pulling and positioning loads.
summary: The Masdaam rope puller kit is a hand-operated, continuous rope winch that gives a small crew real pulling force without a truck or capstan. It pulls rope through the unit with a lever, so the rope length is limited only by the line you bring.
highlights: Hand-operated lever, no engine or power needed
Continuous rope pulling, not limited by drum capacity
Portable kit for backyards and access-restricted sites
Useful for directional felling and pulling leaners
Kit includes the puller and a carry case; check listing for included rope and slings
specs: Use the rope type and diameter specified by Masdaam

body.h: What a rope puller does on a tree job
p: A lot of tree work comes down to pulling. A back-leaner needs help to go where you want it, a hung-up tree needs to come down safely, or a big limb has to be pulled away from a roof as it is lowered. Trucks can pull, but they cannot get into a fenced backyard, and pulling by hand with a crew is slow and hard to control.

The Masdaam continuous rope puller is a portable hand winch. You anchor it to a solid stump or tree, feed rope through it, and work the lever to draw the rope in. Because the rope passes through the unit instead of winding on a drum, you can pull as much rope as you have.

Compared with a come-along or a cable winch, a rope puller is lighter to carry and does not run out of cable halfway through the pull. The rope is softer on the tree than wire, and it is easy to coil and pack away at the end of the day.

Pick an anchor that is stronger than the load you plan to put on it, such as a large sound stump or tree at the base, and attach the puller with a rated sling. Run the rope to the tree you are pulling, attached high enough for good leverage. A redirect pulley lets you set the puller off to the side, out of the line of fall.

Keep the rope path clear of people. Stand at the puller, out of the fall zone, and make sure everyone knows the plan before anyone starts cutting. Tension the rope before the cut so the tree is already being helped in the right direction.

Use rope that matches the puller's specification for diameter and type; the wrong rope can slip or wear the mechanism. Work within the rated load of the puller, the rope, the slings and the anchors. Mechanical advantage systems and redirects multiply forces on anchors, so plan those loads before you pull.
Never use a rope puller to lift or lower people. It is rigging and pulling equipment only.

The kit makes the most sense for small crews and homeowners-turned-pros who need controlled pulling force on sites a truck cannot reach. It is also a good backup when the capstan is on another job. Anyone using it should be trained in felling, rigging forces and the manufacturer's instructions. Pair it with a throw line to set your pull line high in the tree.

Keep the puller clean and dry, check the jaws or grip mechanism for wear, and store the rope in a bag so grit does not get carried into the mechanism. Inspect slings and rope before every pull, and retire anything damaged.

faq.q: How long a rope can the Masdaam puller handle?
faq.a: It pulls rope continuously through the unit, so length is set by the rope you bring, not a drum.

faq.q: Can I use it to help fell a back-leaning tree?
faq.a: Yes, that is a common use, as long as anchors, rope and the puller are rated for the load and the operator is trained.

faq.q: Does it need power?
faq.a: No. It is lever-operated by hand.

name: Notch Ergo Climbers
title: Notch Ergo Climbers: Spikes for Tree Removals
h1: Notch Ergo Climbers
meta: Notch Ergo climbers are tree spikes with an ergonomic shank shaped to follow the leg. A comfortable value pick for removal climbers who spur all day.
tagline: Ergonomic spurs for removal climbers who want comfort without top-tier prices.
summary: Notch Ergo climbers are tree spurs with a shank shaped to follow the inside of your leg, which helps them sit flatter and carry weight more comfortably on long removals. They are a popular value choice for climbers moving up from basic spikes.
highlights: Ergonomically shaped shanks
Replaceable gaffs
Padded straps and pads for all-day wear
Good value for regular removal work
Notch spikes for removals only, never for pruning

p: On a big removal, spurs carry you all day. A shank that fights your leg means sore calves, pressure points and tired ankles by lunch. The Notch Ergo shank is shaped to sit closer to the leg, so pressure spreads out and the gaff points into the tree more naturally.
Notch ergo spikes pair that shape with pads and straps that adjust for most legs and boots. Set the pads so they sit just below the knee and snug the straps so the spur does not rotate.

The Ergo line is a good step up for climbers who started on basic spurs and now spend more days on removals. Notch ergo steel climbers and other versions may be offered, so check the listing for shank material and gaff length before you order.

Keep gaffs sharp to the manufacturer's profile, file in the right direction and never grind them hot. Dull gaffs cut out, and cut-outs cause falls. Inspect shanks, straps and buckles before each use and replace worn straps right away.

Spurs are for removals and emergency rescue only; they wound live trees. Always climb with a lanyard and a second attachment as required by ANSI Z133 and your training. Check out the rest of our aluminum spurs to compare models.

faq.q: Can I use Notch Ergo climbers for pruning?
faq.a: No. Spurs damage live trees and should only be used on removals or for rescue.

faq.q: Are the gaffs replaceable?
faq.a: Yes. Replace gaffs when they are too short to sharpen to the correct profile.

name: Yale Phantom 11mm Climbing Rope, Pink and Black
title: Yale Phantom 11mm Pink Rope for Tree Climbing
h1: Yale Phantom Pink Rope: 11mm Pink and Black Climbing Line
meta: Yale Phantom is a pink rope for tree climbing: 11mm static climbing rope in pink and black, easy to spot in the canopy and well suited to SRS and MRS work.
tagline: An 11mm pink and black static climbing line that is easy to spot in any canopy.
summary: Yale Phantom is a pink rope built for tree climbing: an 11mm static climbing line in a pink and black pattern that stands out against bark and leaves. It suits climbers who want a firm, low-stretch line for SRS ascents and MRS work.
highlights: 11mm static climbing rope
Pink and black pattern, easy to tell apart from rigging lines
Low stretch for efficient SRS ascents
Firm, round construction that runs well in mechanical devices
From Yale Cordage, a long-time US rope maker

p: Color is not just style on a tree crew. A bright pink climbing rope stands out against bark, green leaves and gray skies, so the ground crew always knows which line is the climber's. That matters when there are rigging lines, pull lines and throw lines all hanging from the same tree. Nobody should ever cut, tie off or load the wrong rope.
Pink rope also shows up in brush piles and the truck bed, which makes it harder to leave behind or run over with the chipper.
The rope pink and black pattern also helps when two climbers work the same tree. Each climber can keep track of their own line at a glance.

An 11mm climbing rope is a common size for arborist climbing. It gives a good grip for hand-over-hand work and hitches while still running through most mechanical devices designed for that range. The static, low-stretch construction makes SRS ascents more efficient since less of each step goes into stretching the rope.

Always check that your devices, hitch cord and friction savers are rated for the diameter and construction of the rope. Some devices are fussy about specific ropes. If you climb with a Rope Wrench or other SRS device, test the setup low and confirm it behaves the way the manufacturer says it should.

If you climb mostly MRS on a friction hitch, 11mm gives a solid feel in the hand and plenty of surface for the hitch to bite. On SRS it is a familiar size that most climbers can rig with their existing gear.

New rope can feel stiff and slick. A few climbs, or pulling it through a device on the ground, will break it in. Coil or bag it loosely, keep it off the ground on the job, and store it out of the sun, away from fuel and bar oil. Wash with a rope-specific cleaner when it gets dirty, and let it air dry.
Mark each end with the date of first use. Keep a log of hours or climbs so you know how hard it has worked.

Pick a length that covers the tallest trees you climb with plenty of tail. On SRS the rope must reach the ground from the anchor with extra for tending and rescue; on MRS it must reach the ground doubled.

Climbing rope is life-support gear. It must meet the applicable standard for your use, and you must be trained in how to use and inspect it. Before each climb run the whole length through your hands and look for cuts, glazing, core shots, flat or stiff spots and chemical damage. Retire it when in doubt. Cut out damaged ends only if the remaining length is still safe for the trees you climb. Set lines with a Zing-It throw line and see more in our static climbing rope range.

faq.q: Is an 11mm climbing rope good for SRS?
faq.a: Yes. 11mm static rope is widely used for SRS, provided your devices are rated for that diameter and construction.

faq.q: Why do climbers pick a pink rope?
faq.a: A bright, distinct color makes the climbing line easy to identify and keeps it from being confused with rigging lines.

faq.q: How long does a climbing rope last?
faq.a: It depends on use, care and wear. Inspect before every climb and retire it when damage or heavy wear appears.

name: CAMP Enigma Swivel
title: CAMP Enigma Swivel for Climbing and Rigging Systems
h1: CAMP Enigma Swivel
meta: The CAMP Enigma is a compact swivel that lets carabiners and devices rotate freely, so rope systems untwist instead of kinking. Uses, setup and care tips.
tagline: A compact swivel that takes the twist out of your climbing system.
summary: The CAMP Enigma is a compact swivel that sits between connectors so attached gear can turn freely under load. Climbers use it to stop rope twist in SRS and MRS setups and to keep devices facing the right way.
highlights: Compact swivel with two attachment eyes
Rotates freely under load
Reduces rope twist and kinking
Keeps devices aligned on the bridge
Light enough to leave in your kit

p: Rope twist builds up as you spin on a line, especially on long SRS descents. A swivel lets the gear below it turn independently, so the rope can untwist instead of kinking above your device. It is also handy on a bridge to keep a device facing forward, and in rigging and rescue setups where loads spin.
The CAMP Enigma is small and light, so it does not add much bulk between your connectors.
Swivels also help in rescue and rigging setups where a spinning load can wind lines together. Placed in the right spot, a swivel lets the load turn without twisting the rope above it.

Load the swivel along its main axis between properly oriented connectors, and check that nothing cross-loads. Inspect it before use for cracks, wear, and smooth rotation, and retire it after a fall or if it binds. As part of a life-support system it must meet the applicable standard and be used per the manufacturer's instructions by trained climbers. Compare other swivels before you buy.
Keep it clean and dry, and rinse out grit after climbing in dusty or sandy conditions. A swivel that turns roughly is telling you it needs attention or retirement.

faq.q: What is the CAMP Enigma used for?
faq.a: It lets connected gear rotate freely, which reduces rope twist and keeps devices aligned.

faq.q: Can I use the Enigma in my climbing system?
faq.a: If it is rated for your use, yes. Follow CAMP's instructions and inspect it before every climb.

name: Clogger Zero Ultra Men's Premium Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger Chainsaw Trousers: Zero Ultra Premium Pants
h1: Clogger Chainsaw Trousers: Zero Ultra Men's Premium Pants
meta: Clogger chainsaw trousers at the top of the Zero line. The Zero Ultra pairs light, cool leg protection with premium fabrics and features for climbers.
tagline: The premium Clogger Zero chainsaw pant for climbers who log big hours.
summary: Clogger chainsaw trousers in the Zero Ultra model are the premium version of the light, cool Clogger Zero pant. They are built for climbers who wear saw protection every day and want the most comfort and durability Clogger offers.
highlights: Premium version of the Clogger Zero chainsaw pants
Light, breathable build for warm climbing days
Stretch for high steps and saddle work
Cut protection across the front of the legs
Men's fit

body.h: Zero Ultra vs the standard Zero
p: Clogger zero chainsaw pants built their name on being light enough to wear in summer. The Zero Ultra keeps that core idea and steps up the fabrics and features for climbers who are in saw pants every working day. If your pants wear out at the knees and seat from saddle time, the premium build is worth a look.
Fit them with your saddle and climbing boots on. The seat and thighs should let you step high and sit back without pulling, and the hem should clear spur straps.
Like the rest of the line, the Zero Ultra puts the cut protection across the front of the legs, where nearly all saw contact happens. Check the label for exact coverage and the standard it meets.

Wash per the label to clear out oil and sawdust, and retire the pants after any cut into the protective layer. Saw pants reduce injury but do not replace training, sharp chains and good technique. Compare with the standard Clogger Zero chainsaw pants or ground-only Clogger chaps.
Clogger zero ultra chainsaw pants cost more than the standard pair, so look after them: hang them to dry after wet days, and keep them out of the bed of the truck with the saws.

faq.q: Are Clogger Zero Ultra pants good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. They are designed to be light and flexible enough for all-day saddle work.

faq.q: How do I know when to replace chainsaw trousers?
faq.a: Replace them after any cut into the protective layer or when they are worn through.

name: K&H Red Head Felling Wedge
title: K&H Felling Wedges: Red Head Plastic Felling Wedge
h1: K&H Felling Wedges: Red Head Felling Wedge
meta: K&H felling wedges with a red head: tough plastic wedges for lifting trees over and freeing pinched bars. Will not wreck your chain if you clip one.
tagline: A tough plastic felling wedge that every sawyer should carry in the back pocket.
summary: K&H felling wedges are tough plastic wedges for lifting trees past center and keeping kerfs open while bucking. The red head makes them easy to find in sawdust and leaves.
highlights: Plastic, chain-friendly construction
Red head is easy to spot on the ground
Textured faces resist backing out
Use in pairs or stacked for more lift
Fits in a back pocket or wedge pouch

p: Set a wedge behind the bar as soon as there is room during the back cut so the kerf cannot close on the saw. Driving it in lifts the tree toward the face and helps a near-balanced tree go the direction you planned. When bucking, a wedge keeps the cut open so the bar does not pinch.
Use plastic wedges only. Steel wedges and a running chain are a dangerous combination.
K&H wedges are made of tough plastic that will not ruin your chain if you clip one with the saw. The red head makes them easy to find in sawdust and leaves after a felling cut.

Drive wedges with an axe or felling hammer, not the saw. Stack two for more lift, and carry at least two or three of different sizes. Replace wedges with cracked or mushroomed heads. Wedges cannot fix a bad face cut or a heavy back-leaner; for those, plan a pull line or get help. Keep them with your Husqvarna chainsaw wrench and files, and see more in our wedges section.
Clean sap and dirt off wedges at the end of the day and keep them in a pouch on your belt or in a bucket on the truck. A missing wedge is usually found in the next pile of sawdust.

faq.q: Are red head felling wedges good for big trees?
faq.a: They help, but large or heavy-leaning trees often need several wedges, larger sizes or a pull line.

faq.q: Can I hit a plastic wedge with an axe?
faq.a: Yes, with the poll of an axe or a felling hammer. Replace the wedge when the head mushrooms.

name: Husqvarna Combination Tool Wrench
title: Husqvarna Chainsaw Wrench: Combination Tool (Scrench)
h1: Husqvarna Chainsaw Wrench: Combination Tool
meta: The Husqvarna chainsaw wrench, or scrench, combines a bar nut socket and screwdriver in one tool for chain tension, bar changes, plugs and carb trims.
tagline: The one tool every Husqvarna saw owner should have on the belt.
summary: The Husqvarna chainsaw wrench is a combination socket and screwdriver, the tool most sawyers call a scrench. It handles bar nuts, chain tension and many basic adjustments on Husqvarna saws, and fits easily in a pocket or saw kit.
highlights: Socket end for bar nuts
Screwdriver tip for chain tension and adjustments
Spark plug socket on many versions
Compact enough for a pocket or chaps
Husqvarna original, sized for Husqvarna saws
specs: Husqvarna chainsaws; check socket size for your model

p: Chains stretch as they warm up, bars need flipping and tension needs checking all day. Without the right tool, sawyers end up with a pocket knife on the tension screw and a loose bar nut, which is how bars get damaged and chains come off. The Husqvarna scrench solves that with one compact tool.

Most Husqvarna saws use the same bar nut size across a range of models, so one Husqvarna chainsaw tool covers much of the fleet. Check your saw's manual for the bar nut and plug sizes if you run older or very large saws.
The scrench also serves as a quick check tool. A slightly loose bar nut or a sagging chain is easy to fix in seconds with the tool at hand, rather than waiting for the next fuel stop.

With the saw off and the chain brake on, loosen the bar nuts a turn. Lift the bar nose and turn the tensioning screw with the screwdriver end until the chain sits snug on the bottom of the bar but still pulls around by hand with a gloved hand. Hold the nose up while you tighten the nuts.

Check tension again after the first few cuts on a new chain and after the saw warms up. A cold chain tightened hard can bind as it cools, so loosen it a little before you put the saw away after a hot day.

The same wrench takes the bar off for cleaning the groove and oil holes, flipping the bar to even out wear, and changing chains. On many versions the socket also fits the spark plug, so you can check or swap a plug at the truck when a saw will not start.

Use the screwdriver end gently. It is not a pry bar, and bent tips strip screws. If your saw has adjustable carburetor screws, adjustments should follow the manual and are often best left to a dealer, especially on saws with electronic carburetor control.

Keep the chain tension screw and the bar nut threads clean. Sawdust and pitch packed into the threads make them hard to turn, which is when people strip them. A quick blow-out with compressed air at the end of the day helps.

Wrenches go missing in sawdust and leaf litter all the time. Keep one in your chaps or pocket, one in the saw kit and one in the truck. Pair it with a good set of files such as Pferd round files so you can keep the chain sharp in the field. Always make adjustments with the engine off and wear gloves when handling the chain.
If the socket end starts to round off or the screwdriver tip chips, replace the tool. A worn wrench rounds off bar nuts, which then need replacing.

faq.q: What is a Husqvarna scrench?
faq.a: It is a combination tool with a socket for bar nuts and a screwdriver end for the chain tensioner and other adjustments.

faq.q: Will the Husqvarna chainsaw wrench fit my saw?
faq.a: It fits many Husqvarna models. Check your manual for bar nut and spark plug sizes.

faq.q: How tight should a chainsaw chain be?
faq.a: Snug on the bottom of the bar with no sag, yet still easy to pull around by hand with the brake off and engine stopped.

name: Pferd Classic Round Chainsaw Files, Dozen
title: Pferd File: Classic Round Chainsaw Files, Dozen Pack
h1: Pferd File: Classic Round Chainsaw Files, Dozen
meta: A dozen Pferd round chainsaw files. The Pferd file is a favorite of sawyers for clean, consistent cutters in the field. Match the size to your chain pitch.
tagline: A dozen quality round files for keeping saw chain sharp in the field.
summary: The Pferd file is a go-to for sawyers who sharpen in the field, and this dozen pack keeps the truck, the shop and every saw kit stocked. Classic round files cut cleanly and leave a consistent edge on the cutters.
highlights: Box of 12 round chainsaw files
Cuts cleanly for sharp, consistent cutters
Sized to match common chain pitches
Works with file guides and holders
Dozen pack is better value than singles

p: File diameter must match the chain. The wrong size changes the cutter's hook and dulls faster or grabs. Check the chain's packaging or manufacturer chart; common sizes include 5/32 in., 3/16 in. and 7/32 in. for most saw chain used on tree work.
Use a file holder or guide to keep the angle and depth consistent, and file in one direction, away from you, with steady strokes.

Pferd files are made in Germany and are known among sawyers for a consistent cut from file to file. A dozen pack lets you keep a fresh file in every saw kit and replace them as soon as they start to dull.

body.h: Getting the most from each file
p: Rotate the file a little every few strokes so it wears evenly. Keep files dry and stored in a sleeve so they do not knock against each other and dull. Replace a file as soon as it slides instead of cuts. Lower depth gauges as needed and wear gloves while sharpening. Keep a Husqvarna combination wrench handy for tension checks.

Sharpen little and often. A few strokes per cutter at every fuel stop keeps a chain cutting far better than waiting until the saw starts to smoke and pull to one side. Keep every cutter the same length so the chain runs straight in the cut.

faq.q: What size Pferd file do I need?
faq.a: Match the file diameter to your chain. The chain maker's chart lists the right size.

faq.q: How long does a chainsaw file last?
faq.a: It depends on use, but replace it as soon as it glides over the cutter instead of cutting.
